newsitem.title: UK: Blair to turn attention to tough N. Irish problem.
newsitem.headline: Blair to turn attention to tough N. Irish problem.

text.p: A week after his landslide election victory, British Prime Minister Tony Blair will on Thursday turn his attention to the most intractable problem facing his new Labour government -- how to bring lasting peace to Northern Ireland.
Blair will hold a meeting at his London office with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, who last Friday indicated his pleasure at the British election result.
"We now in Britain have a government with a strong majority (which) will enable it to tackle issues with resolution in regard to Northern Ireland," Bruton said.

Before the election, the Conservatives under John Major were in a minority in the British parliament, provoking worries among Roman Catholics in Northern Ireland that they were dangerously reliant on the Protestant Ulster Unionists for support.
Blair now has a huge 179-seat majority, and political commentators are cautiously optimistic that he could make better progress towards a lasting peace.

Deaglan de Breadun, Northern Ireland editor of the Irish Times, said the fact that Sinn Fein, political arm of the guerrilla Irish Republican Army, won two of Northern Ireland's 18 seats in the British parliament -- its best result in modern times -- was also significant, although the victors plan not to take their seats.
"The election of the new Labour government and the two Sinn Fein MPs would appear to enhance the prospect of an IRA ceasefire sometime over the next four or five months," he said.
Blair on Wednesday sought to reassure the Unionists he would take their interests into account by holding a meeting with the leader of the 10-strong parliamentary party, David Trimble.
His new Northern Ireland secretary, Mo Mowlam, has already had meetings with leaders of the province's other main parties.
Major and Bruton cooperated over the past few years in a joint effort to bring peace to Northern Ireland.
But as Major's position in parliament grew more precarious following by-election defeats, Irish worries that he was in thrall to the Unionists grew.

In February 1995, seven months after the IRA declared a ceasefire in its battle to end British rule over Northern Ireland, Major and Bruton unveiled a joint framework document on a political settlement for the province.
Following the end of the ceasefire a year later, they worked to set up talks between all Northern Irish parties except Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political wing.
British government sources were playing down the possibility of a new initiative emerging from Thursday's Blair-Bruton meeting at which Mowlam will also be present.

They said Bruton just happened to be in Britain, to address a Wednesday night meeting of the Oxford Union, the debating society of England's most prestigious university, and had agreed to see Blair to discuss a range of topics.
"It would be odd if Northern Ireland did not come up, but it is just a quick informal meeting," one source said.
